grand_strategy.reading:
Latvia is the textbook case of Luttwak's weak-state strategy: a country of 1.9
million with a long border and a large Russian-speaking population cannot win
an attritional contest with Russia, so it plays the paradoxical game of making
itself too costly to attack and too connected to be left alone. Every pillar
borrows weight from outside: the Canadian-led brigade and Article 5 for
deterrence, EU money and the escape clause for the budget, German and American
factories for the kit, Lithuania's terminal for the gas. The strategy is
consistent but its cost is dependence on partners whose own commitment is
wavering (US rotation gaps, weapons delays, the Pentagon posture review) and on
an internal politics that has shown it can fall to a single drone: the May 2026
crisis, the 52% turnout and 25% of the vote for two populist parties, one
openly pro-Russian, are the soft flank. Russia is graded adversary because the
Latvian state itself names it the existential threat and a sponsor of terrorism,
not because Riga seeks its regime's end; Belarus is a rival whose pressure is
cheap to apply and costly to stop. Two signals that are not rows: the
Silina government fell over an air-defence failure, not over foreign policy
(Kulbergs, who took over, promised to hold defence at 5% of GDP and keep a hard
line on Moscow), and part of the Russian-speaking population is still outside
the citizenry (non-citizens were 9% of residents in 2024), so the election
measures only part of the minority's weight.

stances.note: The Latvian state itself uses the vocabulary of the mortal enemy: the State Security Service (VDD) puts Russia's services at the head of the threats to the state and a secondary account of its February 2026 report calls Russia an existential threat; the Saeima declared Russia a state sponsor of terrorism on 11 Aug 2022 (67 votes, none against); relations were cut to charge d'affaires level on 24 Feb 2023; and Latvian soil has seen Russian-directed arson cells (cases of 2023-25), GPS jamming from Kaliningrad, and Russian rail crossings shut from 1 Jul 2026. Adversary rather than rival because the declared Latvian aim is Russia's defeat in Ukraine and the Russian state is named the threat to Latvia's existence, not a competitor. The case against: Riga seeks no change of regime in Moscow, keeps an embassy, and still sold EUR 962.5m of goods to Russia in 2025 (4.9% of exports), so the grade is the harder of two readings (the 'rival' reading is the fallback). Bond - grievance: the 1940 occupation and the Soviet deportations, and more than a third of residents who are not ethnic Latvians, mostly Russian-speaking.

stances_toward.note: Latvia suspended the Silene crossing on 19 Sep 2023 and kept it closed (Feb 2024 decision); more than 9,000 illegal-crossing attempts were stopped in 2026, a tunnel was found on 11 Aug 2026, and the Interior Ministry proposed on 4 Aug to suspend Paternieki, the last crossing, as a 'tool of hybrid pressure' - the government declined on 5 Aug. Latvia is a NATO frontline facing the same Belarusian methods as Poland and Lithuania, but there is no personal issue (no Tsikhanouskaya office, no seized trucks), hence stable and bond none. No source uses the word 'rival': our reading (confidence C).

stances_toward.note: Baltic neighbour, NATO and EU co-member, and Lithuania's largest export market (12.4% of exports, Jan-Aug 2025). The three Baltic ministries approved the Baltic Defence Line concept on 19 Jan 2024; Latvia is slower than Estonia on bunkers and has kept its Belarus crossings shut since Sep 2023, while Lithuania reopened after one month in 2025. Latvia and Estonia objected to Lithuania's push for an earlier desynchronisation date (Litgrid's agreement settled on Feb 2025). The Oct 2026 armed incident on the Latvian border with Belarus is a shared frontline issue. Bond - affinity: the Baltic common fate.
